To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
peak bone mass is acquired during childhood and adolescence.

1) the timing of peak bone mass is not well understood and is likely site dependent, with peak bone mass being attained earlier in the hip and femoral neck than in the spine; 2) peak bone mass is acquired during the critical window of time from early to midadolescence; 3) the factors that influence peak bone mass are complex, but include genetic, hormonal, and lifestyle factors.
the attainment of peak BMD is influenced by genetic and environmental factors, with the most important being sex, race, body size, and physical activity.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the factors that influence peak bone mass can be divided into three categories: genetic factors, hormonal determinants, and lifestyle.

the attainment of peak BMD in children is determined by the interplay of genetic and environmental factors, and that the hormonal milieu, particularly sex steroids, is a key determinant of peak bone mass.
there are several hormonal determinants that are responsible for peak bone mass, and that these factors may be altered in a variety of endocrine disorders.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the majority of bone mineral density accrual occurs during puberty, with the most rapid gain in the first 2 yr after onset of puberty.

the peak bone mass is a critical determinant of fracture risk later in life, and therefore it is important to identify those individuals who are at risk of having low bone mass in early life so that preventive strategies can be implemented to optimize peak bone mass.
